themes.theme_label: Quantum kernel classifiers dominate fraud detection approaches
themes.description: A large proportion of papers employ quantum support vector machines or quantum kernel methods as the primary classification mechanism for fraud detection, using quantum feature maps to embed transaction data into high-dimensional Hilbert spaces and computing kernel similarities via state overlaps.
themes.evidence_summary: Papers consistently implement QSVMs using quantum feature maps (ZZFeatureMap, PauliFeatureMap, ZFeatureMap) and quantum kernels computed as state overlaps, applied to credit card, insurance, cross-border, and AML fraud datasets. Implementations range from hardware-efficient circuits on simulators to trapped-ion and superconducting QPU runs, with quantum kernels serving as the most commonly evaluated quantum classification paradigm for fraud.

themes.theme_label: Extreme class imbalance defines fraud dataset challenge
themes.description: Papers consistently identify severe class imbalance as the fundamental obstacle for fraud detection, with fraudulent transactions comprising less than 1% of data in most benchmarks, requiring specialized handling before any classifier can be effective.
themes.evidence_summary: Papers report fraud ratios ranging from 0.172% to about 6%, with many using the European credit card dataset (492 frauds out of 284,807 transactions). Authors repeatedly state that this imbalance causes misleading accuracy metrics, majority-class bias, and difficulty training quantum classifiers that must handle extremely rare positive cases.

themes.description: A large proportion of papers conduct quantum experiments exclusively on noiseless or low-noise simulators, explicitly acknowledging that hardware noise and device constraints could alter reported performance and that results may not transfer to production settings.
themes.evidence_summary: Authors explicitly state that quantum experiments are run on simulators (Qiskit Aer, PennyLane default.qubit, etc.) rather than physical hardware, and caution that real-device behavior may differ substantially. Multiple papers call for future hardware validation as a necessary next step, framing their current results as proof-of-concept rather than deployment-ready evidence.

themes.theme_label: Classical models remain competitive or superior
themes.description: Several papers report that classical ensemble methods such as XGBoost, Random Forest, and gradient boosting outperform or match quantum models on standard fraud detection metrics, indicating that quantum advantage in fraud detection is not yet established.
themes.evidence_summary: Papers report classical XGBoost achieving 89-95% ROC-AUC versus lower quantum scores, Random Forest reaching 97.3% accuracy while QSVM lags behind, classical SVM at 99% vs QSVM at 91-93%, and classical ensemble methods consistently producing the best fraud-class F-measures. Authors attribute this to the maturity of classical methods and the constraints of current quantum hardware.

themes.theme_label: Dimensionality reduction required before quantum encoding
themes.description: Papers consistently apply PCA or other dimensionality reduction techniques to compress transaction features to match available qubit counts, reflecting a fundamental hardware constraint that limits the number of features quantum models can natively process.
themes.evidence_summary: Papers reduce features from 28-30 anonymized PCA components or raw attributes down to 2-10 principal components to match qubit counts. Authors note that limited qubit availability forces aggressive dimensionality reduction before quantum encoding, which may remove discriminative information relevant to fraud detection and constrains the realism of the evaluation.

themes.theme_label: Fraud modeled as unsupervised anomaly detection
themes.description: Multiple papers formulate fraud detection as an unsupervised anomaly detection problem, training models on normal transactions and detecting fraud through deviation from learned normal patterns, using quantum autoencoders, quantum LOF, QSVDD, or one-class quantum SVMs.
themes.evidence_summary: Papers use quantum autoencoders that detect fraud via reconstruction fidelity differences, quantum LOF for k-distance-based outlier scoring, QSVDD for minimum-volume hypersphere enclosure, quantum one-class SVMs, and QUBO-based anomaly selection. The unsupervised framing is motivated by scarce fraud labels and the expectation that most transactions are legitimate, making anomaly-based approaches natural for this domain.

themes.theme_label: Hybrid quantum-classical pipeline architecture for fraud
themes.description: Papers consistently propose architectures where classical components handle data preprocessing, feature engineering, and post-processing while quantum modules perform specific subproblems such as feature mapping, kernel estimation, or ensemble optimization within an end-to-end fraud detection pipeline.
themes.evidence_summary: Papers describe end-to-end hybrid workflows combining classical neural networks with variational quantum circuits, QSVM with XGBoost ensembles, classical LSTM feeding quantum feature maps, and QUBO-based ensemble fusion of quantum and classical classifiers. The hybrid design is motivated by NISQ constraints that prevent fully quantum processing and by the practical need to integrate quantum modules into existing fraud infrastructure.

themes.theme_label: Quantum feature map choice materially affects performance
themes.description: Papers report that the selection of quantum feature map (ZFeatureMap, ZZFeatureMap, PauliFeatureMap, IQP circuits) and encoding parameters significantly impact fraud detection accuracy, with some configurations yielding strong results and others failing to separate classes.
themes.evidence_summary: Papers compare multiple feature maps and report substantial performance differences: ZZFeatureMap with entanglement achieves 94.59% accuracy on insurance fraud while Z maps score lower; QSVC with ZFeatureMap reaches F1 0.98 on credit fraud while PauliFeatureMap shows higher losses; IQP circuits with data re-uploading outperform simpler encodings by 15% in average precision. Feature map choice is reported as one of the most consequential design decisions.

themes.theme_label: Oversampling techniques mitigate fraud class rarity
themes.description: Multiple papers apply SMOTE, Quantum-SMOTE, random oversampling, or class-weighted losses to rebalance training data before quantum model training, reporting substantial improvements in minority-class detection metrics.
themes.evidence_summary: Papers report that SMOTE raises fraud-class recall from 60% to 86.5%, that Quantum-SMOTE with QSVM outperforms traditional undersampling by 6.4 percentage points, and that SMOTE-ENN yields the highest recall under extreme class sparsity. Authors consistently treat class rebalancing as a prerequisite for effective quantum classifier training on fraud data.

themes.description: Papers highlight that fraud detection in modern payment systems requires millisecond-level decision making and high throughput, creating stringent latency constraints that challenge both classical and quantum approaches.
themes.evidence_summary: Papers describe compressed detection-response windows, billions of daily transactions, and that even 50ms of added latency is detrimental in real-time payment contexts. Authors report that quantum circuit execution overhead and cloud-based QPU access introduce latency that can offset speed gains, while operational metrics like inference time per 1,000 transactions are tracked alongside detection quality.

themes.theme_label: Conceptual quantum fraud proposals without empirical validation
themes.description: A substantial group of papers discuss quantum-enhanced fraud detection at a conceptual, review, or survey level without reporting original quantitative experiments, offering prospective claims about potential advantages rather than demonstrated results.
themes.evidence_summary: Papers frame fraud detection as a promising quantum application area and claim benefits such as faster anomaly detection, improved pattern recognition, and reduced false positives, but these claims are presented as qualitative expectations or cited from other work rather than backed by new experiments. Methodological descriptions confirm no datasets, no quantum circuits, and no reproducible benchmarks were produced.

themes.theme_label: Graph-based quantum methods target networked fraud
themes.description: Several papers model fraud detection as a graph problem over transaction networks, applying quantum graph neural networks, quantum community detection, or Gaussian boson sampling to identify coordinated or structurally anomalous fraud patterns.
themes.evidence_summary: Papers represent transactions as graphs where accounts are nodes and transactions are edges, then apply QGNNs for anomaly classification, QUBO-based community detection on CIM hardware to identify high-risk communities containing 70% of fraud, GBS to isolate dense subgraphs corresponding to collusive fraud rings, and hybrid GNN-QNN pipelines for seller fraud ranking. These approaches are motivated by the need to detect coordinated fraud that individual transaction classifiers may miss.

themes.theme_label: Quantum kernels improve with increasing feature dimensionality
themes.description: Papers report that quantum kernel methods, particularly IQP circuits with data re-uploading, show growing performance advantages over classical baselines as the number of features or qubits increases, though experiments remain at 10-20 qubits.
themes.evidence_summary: Papers report that quantum kernels with IQP re-uploading achieve about 15% higher average precision than classical RBF at 20 qubits, that QSVM accuracy advantages widen from small to 3.7 percentage points as qubits increase from 4 to 10, that quantum projected-kernel OCSVMs generalize better with win probabilities above 64%, and that multiple kernel learning overcomes concentration effects that degrade single quantum kernels at higher dimensions.

themes.theme_label: Recall and precision-recall metrics preferred over accuracy
themes.description: Papers consistently argue that accuracy is misleading under extreme class imbalance and adopt recall, F1-score, PR-AUC, average precision, or macro-averaged metrics as primary evaluation criteria for fraud detection performance.
themes.evidence_summary: Papers state that trivial classifiers can reach 99.8% accuracy by predicting all transactions as normal, making accuracy an inappropriate metric. Authors explicitly prioritize recall because missing rare fraudulent cases is costly, use PR-AUC because it is more stringent than ROC-AUC under imbalance, and employ macro averaging to ensure minority-class performance is not masked by majority-class dominance.

themes.theme_label: Hardware noise degrades quantum model performance
themes.description: Papers that test quantum fraud detection models on real quantum hardware or under realistic noise simulations report significant performance degradation compared to noiseless simulation, with some noise channels causing near-random classification.
themes.evidence_summary: Papers report that hardware-executed QSVR shows degraded R² relative to noiseless simulation, that fidelity-histogram overlap on IBM and Rigetti processors makes transaction classification challenging, that bit-flip and bit-phase flip noise reduces fraud classification accuracy from 82% to about 37%, that Sampler QNN performance degrades markedly as noise increases, and that quantum F1 scores fluctuate around simulator values on QPUs. Some papers also show that noise-resilient shallow circuits can maintain partial robustness.
